newsitem.title: FRANCE: CYCLING-BRILLIANT ULLRICH BEARS INDURAIN COMPARISON.
newsitem.headline: CYCLING-BRILLIANT ULLRICH BEARS INDURAIN COMPARISON.

text.p: The abiding image of the 1997 Tour de France is of young German Jan Ullrich conquering Arcalis.
Without once rising from his saddle during the tough ascent of the Andorran mountain, Ullrich snatched the yellow jersey -- and never let go.
Three days later Ullrich painted another memorable picture of his dominance in only his second Tour.
Conjuring up more comparisons with his idol Miguel Indurain, he won the St Etienne time trial to double his overall lead to more than six minutes.
Those two crucial stage victories made Ullrich odds-on to win the Tour even though there was still more than a week's hard riding to come.
"I realised in the Andorra stage that Ullrich definitely had the qualities of a great champion," said his team manager Walter Godefroot.
"Ullrich doesn't understand what's happening to him," the Belgian said. "He is shy and too modest."

But while Ullrich may have surprised many by dominating the world's premier cycling race at only his second attempt, the freckle-faced 23-year-old has made a habit of winning from his very first days on a bike.
And the indications are that he is capable of emulating Indurain's five successive Tour victories or even surpassing the retired Spaniard's achievement.
Ullrich has followed in the footsteps of other Tour greats, Jacques Anquetil, Bernard Hinault and Laurent Fignon, by winning his first classic at 23.
Brought up behind the Iron Curtain in the Baltic port city of Rostock by his mother Marianne after his father left home when he was three, Ullrich showed early sporting promise.
He also showed an interest in cycling, watching the likes of Fignon and Greg LeMond on television, dreaming of the yellow jersey and winning his first race when he was nine.
This promise was recognised by Peter Becker, who persuaded Ullrich to attend the East German national sports school as a boarder when he was 13 and took him on at his Dynamo Berlin cycling club.
In 1993, aged 19, Ullrich won the world amateur championship in Oslo, his first meeting with Godefroot.
A year later he signed as a professional with Telekom with Becker playing a leading part in the negotiations.
Becker still manages Ullrich's remarkable yearly training programme of some 40,000 kms -- 10,000 more than last year's champion Bjarne Riis.
Ullrich spent his first two pro seasons consolidating and was third in the world time trial championship in Sicily in 1994.
The victories disappeared but it was all part of a learning process that culminated in Sunday's glorious success in the greatest race of all.
His mother said: "I'm so happy for my little darling, but I'm worried that things could change."
Becker, however, believes the strong discipline and values instilled in the young man under the old East German system will stand him in good stead under the increasing pressure brought on by fame.

Godefroot said he did not become fully aware of Ullrich's potential until early last year when after a brilliant Dunkirk Four Days race a rival team manager asked him where he had unearthed such a freak.
A very good Tour of Switzerland followed and Godefroot found himself forced to change his plans for the rest of the season.

Originally planning to go to the Olympic Games in Atlanta, he instead took part in the Tour and, after a brilliant penultimate stage time trial in which he eclipsed Indurain, he finished second overall to team mate Riis.
It was then that many, Indurain included, predicted Sunday's victory and more to follow.
